title: Formatting Python Dates with strftime()
learningObjectives: Explain formatting date and time values as readable strings and its role in Python applications.
Choose appropriate datetime classes and methods for formatting date and time values as readable strings.
Predict the output of representative PY17.5 operations.
Identify invalid values, formatting ambiguity or timezone risks related to formatting date and time values as readable strings.

understand.concept: The `strftime()` method converts a date or datetime object into a string using format directives. Directives represent fields such as year, month, day, hour and weekday. Formatting is for display; it does not change the original date-time object.
understand.whyItMatters: Readable and consistent date strings are needed in reports, filenames, user interfaces and logs. Explicit formats reduce ambiguity between regional date conventions.
understand.analogy: Date-time values are like entries on a calendar plus the hands on a clock; a duration measures the distance between two entries.
understand.analogyLimit: Real calendars include leap years, time zones and daylight-saving transitions that a simple wall calendar analogy does not fully model.
understand.summary: Formatting Python Dates with strftime() teaches reliable representation and manipulation of Python date-time values.

explain.narrative:
## Format with strftime
Call `value.strftime(format_string)` to produce a string. Common directives include `%Y` for a four-digit year, `%m` for a zero-padded month, `%d` for day, `%H` for 24-hour hour, `%M` for minute and `%A` for weekday name.

## Choose unambiguous formats
For machine-readable dates, prefer ISO-style `YYYY-MM-DD`. For people, choose a format that matches the audience and label ambiguous values when necessary.

## Formatting is not parsing
`strftime()` formats an existing object. Parsing a string into a datetime uses `strptime()` with a matching format string. Always validate external date strings and handle ValueError.

## Locale considerations
Names such as month and weekday can depend on the active locale. Numeric directives are generally more predictable for tests and data exchange.

examples.title: Format an ISO-style date
examples.code:
from datetime import date
day = date(2026, 11, 19)
print(day.strftime('%Y-%m-%d'))

examples.title: Format a date with a month name
examples.code:
from datetime import date
day = date(2024, 6, 5)
print(day.strftime('%B %d, %Y'))
examples.explanation: %B is the full month name and %d is a zero-padded day.

examples.title: Format a 24-hour time
examples.code:
from datetime import datetime
moment = datetime(2026, 3, 2, 17, 8)
print(moment.strftime('%H:%M'))
examples.explanation: %H and %M format hours and minutes with leading zeros.

examples.title: Format weekday and date
examples.code:
from datetime import date
day = date(2024, 1, 1)
print(day.strftime('%A'))
print(day.strftime('%Y'))
examples.explanation: Weekday names are produced by %A; locale may affect language.

examples.title: Parse a date string with strptime
examples.code:
from datetime import datetime
parsed = datetime.strptime('19-11-2026', '%d-%m-%Y')
print(parsed.date())
examples.explanation: strptime parses text using the matching format directives.
